name: Training Data Curation and Synthetic Data
question: Is my fine-tuning data clean, balanced and safe to train on?
summary: Curation builds the fine-tuning dataset itself: source examples from logs and experts, put them in one label set and one format, remove exact and near duplicates, fix wrong labels, balance intents and languages, scrub personal data, drop anything that overlaps the eval set, and fill thin intents with synthetic examples from a stronger model that are checked before use. A small, clean, consistent set usually beats a large noisy one. The training methods live in SFT, DPO and distillation; proving the result lives in Before and after.
useCases: Turning support, chat or call-centre logs into training data
A task where a few intents dominate and rare ones matter most
Any dataset that may hold customers’ personal data

items.detail: production logs for realism, experts for rare and hard cases; one label set, one format
exact hashes first, then MinHash with LSH for near-copies (Jaccard ≈ 0.8)
confident learning ranks likely errors; people review the hardest ones
cap dominant intents; cover every language and channel you serve
scrub identifiers before training; drop rows that match the eval set
written by a stronger model, then filtered, verified and spot-checked

steps: Pull logs and expert examples into one label set and one format
Deduplicate, then decontaminate against the eval set
Clean labels with model help and human review; scrub PII; rebalance
Fill thin intents with verified synthetic rows, and version the dataset
pitfalls: Training on raw logs, so copies, wrong labels and personal data go straight into the weights
Deduplicating within the training data only, leaving eval items in it
Unchecked synthetic rows that repeat the generator’s mistakes and sameness
remember: Fewer, cleaner, balanced rows: dedup, decontaminate, fix labels, scrub PII, verify the synthetic ones.
caption: Illustrative: 50,000 logged loan queries at Udaan Lend, a fictional NBFC, curated to 37,480 rows.

steps.title: Source and normalise
steps.text: Udaan Lend, a fictional NBFC, pulls 50,000 loan queries from 14 months of chat and call-centre logs, plus a few hundred replies written by collections and grievance experts. normalise() maps old label spellings onto one set of 12 intents and puts every row in the same chat format, so the model never sees “EMI date” and “emi_due_date” as two different answers.

steps.title: Remove exact and near duplicates
steps.text: A SHA-256 hash catches exact copies. MinHash signatures on 5-character shingles, indexed with LSH, catch near-copies at Jaccard similarity 0.8, such as the same template with a different name. 9,000 rows, 18%, go. Copies over-weight a few phrasings and waste review effort.

steps.title: Decontaminate against the eval set
steps.text: The same signatures are checked against the 2,000-item eval set. 400 training rows are near-copies of eval items. Left in, the model memorises them: on the raw data the full eval set reports 84.9% while its 1,600 clean items show 81.4%. Removing them leaves 40,600 rows.

steps.title: Find and fix wrong labels
steps.text: find_label_issues compares each logged intent with cross-validated predictions and ranks the likely errors. The 2,000 hardest go to trained reviewers at ₹40 each, ₹80,000 in all; clear-cut ones are relabelled by a stronger model. Wrong labels fall from 9% to about 1.5%.

steps.title: Scrub PII, then rebalance
steps.text: 12% of rows carry Aadhaar or PAN numbers, mobile numbers, names or loan account numbers. A model can repeat what it was trained on, and India’s DPDP Act expects personal data to be used only for a stated purpose, so scrub_pii() swaps them for typed placeholders such as [PAN], catching 98%. Then the EMI-due-date intent, 30% of rows, is cut to one in three: 8,120 rows go and 32,480 remain.

steps.title: Add verified synthetic rows
steps.text: Three rare intents, foreclosure quotes, restructuring requests and grievance escalation, have about 1,200 real rows. A stronger model writes 8,000 more in English, Hindi and Hinglish; checks keep 5,000 where an independent classifier agrees, facts match the policy sheet and nothing copies a real or eval row, and reviewers spot-check 500 for ₹20,000. Rare-intent accuracy rises from 58% to 87%, and overall to 90.6% on 37,480 rows.

pros: Fewer, cleaner rows often beat many noisy ones, and train faster
Scrubbing keeps customers’ personal data out of the weights
Verified synthetic rows fill intents the logs barely cover
cons: Human review costs money and time: ₹80,000 for 2,000 rows here
Thresholds for near-duplicates and label issues need tuning
Synthetic rows can carry the generator’s errors and sameness
Every new log batch needs the same pipeline again
avoidWhen: A prompt or retrieval already meets the bar, so there is nothing to train (see Decide)
You have no held-out eval set yet, so you cannot tell whether curation helped

practice.scenario: Udaan Lend, a fictional NBFC, wanted a small model to classify and answer loan queries. Its first tuning run used 50,000 raw chat and call-centre logs and scored 84.9% on the eval set, which looked fine until an audit found 400 eval items copied in the training data; on clean items the score was 81.4%, and foreclosure and grievance queries were right only 58% of the time. The team deduplicated with MinHash, removed the eval overlap, fixed labels with cleanlab and 2,000 human reviews, scrubbed PII, capped the EMI-date intent and added 5,000 verified synthetic rows for rare intents. The new set had 37,480 rows, and the model scored 90.6% honestly, with 87% on rare intents.

practice.analogy: Preparing a revision guide from a year of class notes: throw out the photocopies of the same page, correct the wrong answers, black out classmates’ phone numbers, remove the actual exam questions, and write a few extra worked examples for the chapters nobody took notes on.

library.name: datasketch and cleanlab
library.what: MinHash LSH finds near-duplicates and eval overlap; confident learning ranks rows whose labels are probably wrong.

practice.note: scrub_pii() is a regex sketch; names and addresses need an NER-based tool such as Microsoft Presidio, plus a human check on a sample. The loan account format UL followed by 10 digits is invented for this example. Label-issue ranking uses cleanlab.filter.find_label_issues with cross-validated probabilities. This is educational material, not legal advice on the DPDP Act.

samples.code:
import hashlib
import re
from datasketch import MinHash, MinHashLSH

def sig(text, n=5, num_perm=128):
    """MinHash signature over character 5-grams of normalised text."""
    text = " ".join(text.lower().split())
    m = MinHash(num_perm=num_perm)
    for i in range(max(1, len(text) - n + 1)):
        m.update(text[i:i + n].encode("utf-8"))
    return m

def dedupe(rows, threshold=0.8):
    lsh, seen, kept = MinHashLSH(threshold=threshold, num_perm=128), set(), []
    for i, r in enumerate(rows):
        h = hashlib.sha256(" ".join(r["text"].lower().split()).encode()).hexdigest()
        m = sig(r["text"])
        if h in seen or lsh.query(m):
            continue                       # exact or near copy
        seen.add(h)
        lsh.insert(f"row-{i}", m)
        kept.append(r)
    return kept

def decontaminate(rows, eval_rows, threshold=0.8):
    lsh = MinHashLSH(threshold=threshold, num_perm=128)
    for j, e in enumerate(eval_rows):
        lsh.insert(f"eval-{j}", sig(e["text"]))
    return [r for r in rows if not lsh.query(sig(r["text"]))]

PII = [("AADHAAR", re.compile(r"\b\d{4}\s?\d{4}\s?\d{4}\b")),
       ("PAN", re.compile(r"\b[A-Z]{5}\d{4}[A-Z]\b")),
       ("MOBILE", re.compile(r"(?:\+91[\s-]?)?\b[6-9]\d{9}\b")),
       ("EMAIL", re.compile(r"\b[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+\b")),
       ("LOAN_AC", re.compile(r"\bUL\d{10}\b"))]

def scrub_pii(text):
    for tag, pattern in PII:
        text = pattern.sub(f"[{tag}]", text)
    return text

def cap_intent(rows, intent, keep_every=3):
    out, n = [], 0
    for r in rows:
        if r["intent"] == intent:
            n += 1
            if n % keep_every:
                continue                   # keep 1 in 3
        out.append(r)
    return out

numericDrill.question: Udaan Lend has 50,000 logged loan queries. Deduplication removes 18% of them, decontamination then removes 400 rows that match the eval set, and the EMI-date intent, 30% of what remains, is cut to one row in three. Finally 5,000 verified synthetic rows are added. How many rows is the final training set?
numericDrill.answer: 50,000 × 0.82 = 41,000 after deduplication; 41,000 − 400 = 40,600. The EMI-date intent is 0.3 × 40,600 = 12,180 rows; keeping one in three leaves 4,060, so 8,120 go and 32,480 remain. Adding 5,000 synthetic rows gives 37,480, fewer than the 50,000 raw rows but a better model.

interview.question: How would you build a fine-tuning dataset from production logs?
interview.answer: Pull logs and expert-written examples into one label set and one format. Deduplicate exactly and with MinHash for near-copies, and remove anything that overlaps the eval set. Rank likely label errors with a tool like cleanlab and have people review the hardest ones. Scrub personal data, rebalance dominant intents and languages, and fill thin intents with synthetic rows from a stronger model that are filtered and spot-checked. Version the dataset and measure every change on a clean held-out set.

interview.question: When is synthetic data a good idea, and what can go wrong?
interview.answer: It helps when real examples of an intent, language or edge case are scarce, or cannot be used for privacy reasons. It goes wrong when rows are used unchecked: the generator’s factual errors, a narrow style that differs from real users, and copies of eval items all pass into training, and repeated rounds of training on generated data can narrow what a model produces. Generate from a stronger model, verify with an independent classifier, rules and a human sample, deduplicate against real and eval data, and keep real data as the backbone.

mistakes.mistake: Deduplicating the training data but never checking it against the eval set
mistakes.fix: Run the same near-duplicate check between training rows and eval items, and drop the overlaps from training

mistakes.mistake: Adding generated rows straight from the model
mistakes.fix: Filter with independent checks and a human spot-check, and track how many are rejected

quiz.question: An NBFC has 50,000 logged loan queries, and 18% are exact or near copies. How many rows remain after deduplication?
Which technique finds near-duplicate messages, such as the same template with a different customer name, without comparing every pair?
options: SHA-256 hashing only
MinHash signatures with locality-sensitive hashing
Sorting by message length
Removing stop words
quiz.explanation: Hashes only catch exact copies; MinHash with LSH estimates Jaccard similarity and finds near-copies efficiently.

quiz.question: A tuned claims classifier scores 92% on the eval set, but 300 eval items also appear in the training data. What is the most likely effect?
options: The score is inflated because the model memorised those items
The score is deflated
No effect, because the eval set is stored separately
The model will refuse those items
quiz.explanation: Contamination rewards memorisation; score the model on clean items and remove the overlap from training.

quiz.question: 400 of 2,000 eval items were in training and are answered 99% correctly; the other 1,600 score 81.4%. What does the full eval set report?
A UPI help-desk dataset will be used for fine-tuning. Which should be scrubbed or replaced with placeholders? Select all that apply.
options: Mobile numbers
Full bank account numbers
The intent label, such as refund_status
UPI IDs that identify a person
quiz.explanation: Identifiers of people and accounts are personal data; the intent label is what the model must learn.

quiz.question: Why is it risky to fine-tune on patient messages that still contain names and phone numbers?
options: It makes training slower
A model can reproduce training text, so personal data can leak in its outputs
Names confuse the tokenizer
It lowers accuracy on every task
quiz.explanation: Models can memorise and repeat rare strings from training data; remove identifiers first.

quiz.question: A label-issue tool flags 6,000 rows, and the budget allows people to review 2,000 at ₹40 each. What does the review cost?
What does confident learning, as in cleanlab, use to find probable label errors?
options: The length of each example
Out-of-sample predicted probabilities compared with the given labels
The order rows were logged in
Random sampling only
quiz.explanation: Where a model trained on other folds is confidently in disagreement with the label, the label is probably wrong.

quiz.question: 30% of 40,600 support rows are one intent. If you keep one in three of that intent, how many rows remain in total?
quiz.explanation: The intent has 12,180 rows; keeping 4,060 removes 8,120, leaving 32,480.

quiz.question: Which checks make generated rows safe to add for rare loan intents? Select all that apply.
options: An independent classifier agrees with the intent
Facts are checked against the current policy sheet
Near-copies of real or eval rows are removed
The generator rates its own rows as correct
quiz.explanation: Self-rating by the same model is not independent; use separate checks and a human spot-check.

quiz.question: A stronger model generates 8,000 rows and checks keep 5,000. What is the rejection rate?
A team has 50,000 noisy rows or 37,480 curated rows. What does experience, such as the LIMA study, suggest?
options: More rows always win
A smaller, cleaner, well-chosen set often matches or beats a larger noisy one
Row count does not matter at all
Only synthetic rows matter
quiz.explanation: Quality and diversity matter more than raw volume for teaching behaviour and format.

quiz.question: A Hindi and Hinglish chatbot’s training data is 90% English. What is the best curation step?
options: Delete the Hindi rows
Balance languages to match the users served, adding verified Hindi and Hinglish rows if needed
Translate everything into English
Nothing: the model will generalise
quiz.explanation: The dataset should cover every language and channel the model will serve.

quiz.question: Deduplication is run within the training data only. What problem remains?
options: Exact copies in training
Near-copies between training and the eval set
Wrong labels are removed
PII is scrubbed
quiz.explanation: Decontamination is a separate check against the eval set, using the same signatures.

quiz.question: Which are signs a fine-tuning dataset needs curation before training? Select all that apply.
options: One intent is 30% of the rows
The same template appears thousands of times
Two teams used different label names for the same intent
Every intent has a similar number of clean examples
quiz.explanation: Skew, copies and inconsistent labels are all curation problems; balanced, clean intents are the goal.

quiz.question: The same intent is labelled refund_status, RefundStatus and ‘refund status’ in three log sources. What should happen first?
options: Train on them as three intents
Map them onto one label before any other step
Drop two of the sources
Let the model learn the variants
quiz.explanation: Label and format consistency comes first; otherwise the model learns three answers for one question.

quiz.question: 12% of 40,600 rows hold PII, and a scrubber catches 98%. About how many rows still hold PII?
quiz.explanation: 40,600 × 0.12 = 4,872; 2% of 4,872 ≈ 97. A second pass or a sample review catches the rest.

quiz.question: A model is trained repeatedly on its own generated product answers, round after round. What is the known risk?
options: Model collapse: outputs grow narrower and rare cases fade
The model becomes too creative
Training becomes free
Nothing, if the model is large
quiz.explanation: Keep real data as the backbone and verify generated rows.

quiz.question: Which belong in a dataset card for a curated fine-tuning set? Select all that apply.
options: Sources and time period
Deduplication and decontamination thresholds
Share of synthetic rows and how they were verified
The reviewers’ personal phone numbers
quiz.explanation: Record how the set was built so it can be rebuilt and audited; never personal data of reviewers.

quiz.question: Rare-intent accuracy rises from 58% to 87% after curation. By how many percentage points did it improve?
